strengths: The paper presents a simple and potentially useful formulation: predicting a small set of scene-conditioned polynomial coefficients to convert frozen monocular-depth output into metric depth using sparse radar guidance.

The empirical results are substantial and consistent across three radar-camera datasets and three evaluation ranges. PolyRad outperforms all five reported baselines in every entry of Table 1, often by large margins, particularly on ZJU-4DRadarCam.

The evaluation includes four different monocular-depth backbones. PolyRad improves upon both the raw predictions and RadarCam-Depth for every backbone in Table 2, providing evidence that the approach is not tied exclusively to UniDepth.

The polynomial-degree study establishes that nonlinear mappings materially outperform the learned scale-and-shift case, while the degradation at degree 10 usefully demonstrates the anticipated flexibility-versus-stability tradeoff.
The component ablations support the utility of radar prototypes, cross-modal attention, and derivative regularization. The method is also conceptually compact and clearly described at a high level.
weaknesses: The central geometric claims are overstated. PolyRad applies one global scalar function f(z) to every pixel, so pixels or objects having the same input depth must receive the same output depth regardless of spatial or semantic context. Moreover, a monotonic f cannot reverse any incorrect depth ordering. It can adjust depth-dependent spacing, but it cannot generally repair the cross-object ordering errors used to motivate the method or make localized corrections to object boundaries as repeatedly claimed.

The proposed derivative loss does not actually enforce monotonicity: softly penalizing |1-f'(z)| encourages an identity slope but permits negative derivatives. No measurements of monotonicity violations or comparison with a genuine constraint such as positive derivative parameterization or isotonic fitting are given. Setting the target slope to 1 is also dependent on the arbitrary scale and parameterization of each MDE output, yet the normalization needed to make this meaningful is not specified.

The interpretation through inflection points is technically imprecise. A degree-N polynomial has at most N-2 real inflection points, and roots of f'' are only inflection points when curvature changes sign. Higher-order coefficients also do not inherently correspond to finer, local, or object-specific corrections. These issues weaken the claimed principled geometric explanation, although they do not invalidate the empirical model.

The experiments do not isolate whether the gains arise from polynomial fitting itself or from the learned radar-depth fusion network and dense depth supervision. Important controls are missing, including robust per-scene polynomial or monotonic-spline fitting directly to radar/depth correspondences, and an equally parameterized nonlinear regressor without the polynomial interpretation.

Reproducibility is limited in the provided manuscript: dataset splits and preprocessing, radar accumulation and filtering, depth normalization, architecture dimensions, polynomial stabilization, loss weights, training schedule, and baseline retraining protocol are deferred to an unavailable supplement or omitted. Runtime and parameter comparisons are also absent despite efficiency claims.

The quantitative evidence lacks repeated-run variability or statistical uncertainty. The sparse qualitative error visualizations provide no color scale, and no failure cases or adverse-weather breakdowns are shown despite robustness being part of the radar motivation.

Several headline improvement figures are inconsistent or insufficiently defined: the abstract reports 30.3% MAE and 37.2% RMSE, the introduction reports dataset improvements of 11.3%, 54.6%, and 35.2%, and Section 4.1 reports yet another set of metric-specific percentages. The aggregation and comparison points should be stated explicitly. Overall, the strong multi-dataset results place the work near the acceptance boundary, but the mismatch between the global mapping's actual capabilities and the paper's principal claims, together with missing decisive controls and implementation details, prevents a clear acceptance recommendation.

strengths: The core idea is simple and potentially useful: predict scene-specific coefficients from sparse radar and apply a nonlinear transformation to a frozen monocular-depth prediction.

The reported results are substantial and consistent across three radar-camera datasets. Table 1 shows improvements over all five evaluated baselines at 50 m, 70 m, and 80 m, rather than only on a single benchmark or operating range.
The degree study in Table 3 provides evidence that nonlinear transformations outperform scale-and-shift, while the backbone study indicates that the approach is not tied exclusively to UniDepth.
The manuscript is generally readable, and the overall pipeline and motivation are communicated clearly through the main figures and equations.
weaknesses: The evidence does not isolate polynomial fitting as the source of the gains. The method also introduces learned radar prototypes, cross-modal attention, a CNN, and supervised scene-level coefficient prediction, but it is not compared with similarly parameterized alternatives such as an MLP mapping, monotone spline, piecewise-linear mapping, or lookup table. Table 3 only compares different polynomial degrees within the proposed system, so the central representation choice remains weakly justified.

Several mathematical claims are inaccurate or overstated. A degree-N polynomial has at most N-2 inflection points, and a quadratic has none, contrary to the repeated suggestion that each additional order introduces an inflection point. The claim that the polynomial's degrees of freedom are close to the radar-point cardinality is also inconsistent with the reported degree 8: nine coefficients are not close to the stated hundreds of radar points.

The proposed regularizer does not enforce monotonicity. Penalizing |1-f'(z)| encourages slopes near one but does not guarantee f'(z) >= 0, positive output depth, or absence of oscillations. No measurements of monotonicity violations, negative depths, coefficient magnitudes, or extrapolation stability are reported. This matters especially for an unnormalized eighth-degree polynomial, whose numerical behavior is not described.

A single global function of input depth cannot distinguish pixels or objects having the same MDE value but requiring different metric depths. If the transformation is monotone, it also cannot change global ordinal relationships at all. This substantially narrows the method's corrective capacity relative to the manuscript's claims about resolving arbitrary cross-object misalignment, recovering boundaries, and making local corrections.

Essential experimental and implementation information is absent from the provided manuscript: dataset splits, ground-truth construction and validity masks, training schedule, loss weights, depth normalization, coefficient/output constraints, prototype and feature dimensions, preprocessing, and baseline retraining protocol. Ground-truth depth in these automotive datasets is sparse, yet Eq. 8 is written over a dense H-by-W map without explaining masking. The repeated reliance on an unavailable supplement prevents adequate reproducibility assessment.

Baseline fairness is difficult to determine. The paper does not state whether all methods were retrained with identical splits, inputs, resolution, supervision, and evaluation masks. It cites relevant radar-depth methods such as CAFNet but omits them from the comparison, and it provides no simple learned nonlinear calibration baseline or oracle fitting baseline.

Reported improvement summaries are internally inconsistent. The abstract reports 30.3% MAE and 37.2% RMSE, the introduction reports dataset figures of 11.3%, 54.6%, and 35.2%, and Section 4.1 reports yet another set of percentages. Several of these do not directly follow from a consistent comparison against the best Table 1 baseline, reducing confidence in the quantitative claims.

The evaluation reports only MAE/RMSE point estimates, without uncertainty across runs, computational cost, parameter count, latency, radar corruption studies, or evaluation under the adverse-weather conditions used to motivate radar. The ablations cover selected modules but do not examine the method's main failure modes or stability across polynomial degrees and datasets.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, intuitive, and potentially useful formulation: scene-conditioned polynomial calibration of pretrained monocular depth predictions using sparse radar. This is a meaningful alternative to heavier dense-fusion pipelines.

The empirical results are strong and consistent across nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft. PolyRad achieves the best reported MAE and RMSE at nearly every evaluated distance, with especially large gains on ZJU and View-of-Delft.
The comparison across four monocular depth backbones is valuable: PolyRad improves DPT, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, and UniDepth, suggesting that the approach is not tied to one pretrained model.

The degree study supports the central hypothesis: performance improves substantially from a linear transformation through degree eight and then slightly degrades at degree ten. The component ablations also show meaningful contributions from radar prototypes, cross-modal attention, and derivative regularization.

The method is clearly motivated and described, and the visualizations make the distinction between global linear calibration and nonlinear depth-dependent correction easy to understand. Leveraging inexpensive radar together with foundation-model priors has clear practical relevance.
weaknesses: The claimed monotonicity guarantee is technically inaccurate. Penalizing |1-f'(z)| encourages a unit slope but does not enforce f'(z) >= 0; negative derivatives and ordering reversals remain possible. The manuscript provides neither a positivity constraint nor measurements of derivative violations or preserved depth ordering. Calling this akin to isotonic regression overstates what the loss establishes.

The model predicts one global polynomial per image. Consequently, pixels with the same monocular prediction must receive the same corrected depth, regardless of object identity or spatial location. It therefore cannot generally resolve object-specific misalignments or refine boundaries as some of the discussion claims. The paper should delimit this representational restriction and directly test the cross-object correction hypothesis.

A slope target of one is sensitive to the arbitrary scale and parameterization of the MDE output, particularly because some backbones produce inverse depth while others produce metric depth. The manuscript does not describe the normalization that makes high powers and the derivative penalty numerically meaningful, nor explain why unit slope is appropriate across backbones.

Reproducibility is presently weak. The provided manuscript repeatedly refers to supplementary material that is absent and omits dataset splits, ground-truth construction and valid-pixel masks, radar preprocessing and point counts, input resolution, feature dimensions, number of prototypes, loss weights, optimizer, schedule, augmentations, coefficient parameterization, and training cost.

The evaluation lacks runtime, parameter, FLOP, and memory comparisons, so the claim of negligible overhead or greater efficiency than complex fusion systems is not demonstrated. Only the final polynomial evaluation is plainly cheap; the added encoders and attention modules may not be.

Several headline improvement percentages differ across the abstract, contribution summary, and main-results discussion, without stating whether they are averaged over datasets, metrics, or distance thresholds. The comparison protocol also needs clearer confirmation that baselines use identical splits, resolutions, radar inputs, and tuning.

The evidence for robustness is limited to aggregate MAE/RMSE and three qualitative examples. There are no uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, adverse-weather subsets, radar sparsity/noise tests, or quantitative diagnostics of oscillation and monotonicity. Thus, the adverse-condition and stability motivations remain insufficiently validated.

strengths: The core idea is simple, original in this application, and practically useful: predicting a scene-specific nonlinear mapping from frozen monocular-depth output to metric depth offers a substantially lower-dimensional alternative to decoding an entirely new dense map.

The empirical results are strong and reasonably broad. POLAR is evaluated on nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft at three distance thresholds, with especially large improvements on ZJU and View-of-Delft and smaller but consistent gains over TacoDepth on nuScenes.

The experiments include meaningful supporting evidence beyond the main benchmark table: polynomial-degree sensitivity, component ablations, four MDE backbones, radar-density degradation, zero-shot cross-dataset transfer, learned-point controls, and comparisons with isotonic, spline, and adapter baselines.

The degree ablation directly supports the principal hypothesis: degree 8 substantially improves over affine fitting on both nuScenes (MAE 2156.8 to 1407.8) and ZJU (1078.2 to 629.6), while the degradation at degree 10 appropriately exposes the flexibility/stability tradeoff.

The method is computationally attractive. The reported 24.81 ms latency and 89.70 GFLOPs improve upon TacoDepth's 29.30 ms and 139.87 GFLOPs, while the polynomial evaluation itself adds negligible overhead. The manuscript is generally clear and provides helpful qualitative comparisons.
weaknesses: The interpretation overstates what the global polynomial can correct. For each scene, the output is a single scalar function of the initial depth, so pixels with equal MDE values necessarily receive equal metric values regardless of location or object identity. It can correct depth-dependent calibration errors, but not arbitrary cross-region misalignments. Claims that higher-order terms provide spatially local corrections or sharpen boundaries are therefore not generally justified by Eq. 5.

The theoretical argument is weak and its corollary is too broad. Proposition 1 merely constructs values that are not affinely related; it does not establish that monocular-depth ambiguity generally has this form. Moreover, Taylor approximation requires metric depth to be a smooth, single-valued function of predicted depth, which need not hold when distinct objects share the same predicted value. The construction consequently does not justify arbitrary cross-object correction.

The stated monotonicity guarantee is inaccurate. The loss penalizes |1-f'(z)| rather than directly constraining f'(z) to be nonnegative, so finite loss does not ensure monotonicity or 'piecewise monotonicity.' Output positivity is likewise not guaranteed. The paper should report derivative violations, negative-depth frequency, or constrained alternatives; the Kendall-tau result is useful but only an indirect aggregate check.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as input-depth normalization for numerically sensitive eighth-degree powers, coefficient parameterization, prototype count, feature dimensions, temperature, encoder/CNN architecture, optimizer, batch size, augmentation, and full dataset split/preprocessing specifications are missing. Equation 2 also has inconsistent stated dimensions/indexing and leaves the softmax axis unclear.

The fairness and scope of the efficiency and accuracy comparisons need clearer documentation. It is not stated consistently whether every baseline was retrained under identical resolutions, splits, hardware, and MDE backbones or whether some numbers were imported. POLAR uses UniDepth for its headline results, and although the appendix gives a useful same-backbone comparison with RadarCam-Depth, equivalent controlled comparisons are absent for the strongest TacoDepth baseline. The nuScenes advantage over TacoDepth is modest, particularly at 50 m (RMSE 2475.7 versus 2487.5), with no variance or significance estimates.

Evaluation uses only MAE and RMSE against sparse projected depth. Boundary-sensitive, relative-order, and standard depth-threshold metrics would better substantiate claims about preserved geometry, boundary sharpening, and local ordinality. The bootstrap two-sample t-test on Kendall tau is also insufficiently specified and appears less appropriate than a paired procedure.

strengths: The paper studies a useful practical problem and proposes an efficient scene-level calibration approach that is considerably simpler than dense radar-camera decoding architectures.

The empirical scope is substantial: results are reported on nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft, with multiple distance thresholds, MDE backbones, component ablations, radar-density tests, zero-shot transfer, and qualitative comparisons.

Reported performance is strong, especially on ZJU and View-of-Delft, and the measured 24.81 ms latency and 89.70 GFLOPs suggest practical value if the comparisons use matched implementations and accounting.

The polynomial-degree study supports the basic empirical premise that nonlinear calibration improves over an affine transformation; degree 8 substantially reduces error relative to degree 1 on both reported datasets.
The manuscript is generally organized and provides intuitive motivation for nonlinear calibration.
weaknesses: The central claimed capability is technically overstated. Equation 5 applies one scene-level scalar function f(z) to every pixel. Consequently, pixels or objects with the same MDE value necessarily receive the same output, irrespective of spatial region. If f is monotone, it preserves every global depth ordering and therefore cannot correct the cross-object inversions emphasized in the motivation; if it is non-monotone, reversals depend only on z and still cannot be region-specific. Radar changes the coefficients per scene but does not remove this structural limitation. Claims that the method makes spatially distinct local corrections, sharpens boundaries, or preserves local ordering while changing cross-region ordering are not established by the formulation.

The proposed monotonicity term does not enforce monotonicity. The penalty ||1-f'(z)||_1 encourages a unit derivative, whereas an actual monotonicity constraint would penalize negative derivatives. Negative slopes remain possible at finite loss, positive slopes far from one are unnecessarily penalized, and no positivity or range constraint on predicted depth is given. Evaluation of the derivative distribution or frequency of negative predictions/inversions is absent.

The theoretical section is largely a non sequitur. Showing that three arbitrary point pairs need not be collinear only proves that an affine function cannot interpolate arbitrary data exactly; it does not establish a misconception about monocular scale ambiguity. The Taylor-expansion argument additionally assumes that ground-truth depth is a smooth single-valued function of predicted depth, precisely the assumption that can fail when different spatial regions share the same prediction but require different corrections.

The empirical evidence does not isolate polynomial fitting from the learned fusion network. The degree-1 ablation shows nonlinear terms help within POLAR, but there is no capacity-matched learned scalar-function baseline such as an MLP, rational function, or learned monotone spline. The reported isotonic/PCHIP/Hermite baselines are post-hoc fits to projected radar points and are insufficiently specified, so they are not controlled alternatives to the end-to-end model.

There is a serious numerical inconsistency in Table 6: the stated no-ablation View-of-Delft result is 629.6/1171.3, exactly the ZJU result elsewhere, while the main View-of-Delft result is 1500.1/3951.8. This makes the View-of-Delft ablation conclusions unverifiable from the manuscript. Other headline improvement percentages also vary across the abstract, introduction, and experiments without a clearly defined averaging procedure.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a high-degree polynomial method. The manuscript omits key architectural and training details such as the number of prototypes, feature dimensions, temperature, exact encoders/MLPs/CNN, input-depth normalization, coefficient parameterization, numerical stabilization for eighth powers, augmentations, valid-pixel handling, and dataset-specific polynomial choices. These details are essential because raw MDE scales and high powers can vary dramatically.

The accuracy and efficiency comparisons need stronger controls. It is unclear whether all baselines use identical splits, image resolutions, backbone accounting, preprocessing, and hardware/software implementations. No repeated-run variation is reported despite several nuScenes gains being modest—for example, at 50 m the RMSE changes only from 2487.5 to 2475.7. The bootstrap-sample two-sample t-test for Kendall correlation also treats resampled estimates as if they were independent observations and is not a convincing significance analysis.

Evaluation is performed at sparse lidar-valid locations, yet the paper repeatedly makes claims about dense high-fidelity reconstruction and recovery of entire surfaces. The qualitative figures cannot validate accuracy in unlabeled regions, and no boundary, ordinal, or dense-surface metric directly supports those claims. Overall, the strong reported numbers and efficiency are worthwhile, but the mismatch between the formulation and its main explanatory claims, combined with uncontrolled baselines, an inconsistent ablation table, and missing reproducibility details, currently makes the evidence insufficient for acceptance.

strengths: POLAR offers a simple and useful reframing of radar-camera depth estimation: it predicts a scene-conditioned polynomial that converts frozen monocular-depth estimates to metric depth. This is more constrained and computationally economical than decoding an unrestricted dense map.

The empirical evidence is broad: experiments cover nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft; compare against recent radar-camera methods; test four MDE backbones; and include polynomial-degree, component, radar-density, cross-dataset, and regression-baseline studies.

The reported accuracy is compelling overall. POLAR is best across the main evaluation settings, with especially large improvements on ZJU and View-of-Delft. The smaller but consistent nuScenes gains over TacoDepth further support the method's competitiveness.

The method is efficient: the reported 24.81 ms latency and 89.70 GFLOPs improve upon TacoDepth's 29.30 ms and 139.87 GFLOPs, while training time is substantially lower than the listed baselines. This strengthens its practical relevance.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, and the degree ablation supports the central claim that a nonlinear transformation improves materially over scale-and-shift fitting.
weaknesses: The global transformation d=f(z) has a fundamental limitation that is understated: pixels with the same MDE value must receive the same output regardless of location or radar correspondence. Thus it cannot generally correct arbitrary cross-region misalignments, create missing geometry, or sharpen boundaries as claimed; it can only correct errors that are approximately a single-valued function of the initial depth within each scene. The construction in Appendix H proves only that affine fitting can fail, not that a global polynomial resolves the general cross-region problem.

The proposed 'monotonicity' loss is not actually a monotonicity constraint. Penalizing |1-f'(z)| encourages unit slope, whereas monotonicity only requires f'(z)>=0. The distinction is consequential because the penalty is scale- and parameterization-dependent. The paper also does not specify normalization or numerical stabilization for degree-8 powers, leaving uncertainty about behavior across MDE backbones and depth ranges.

Some reported evidence is internally inconsistent. In Table 6, the purported View-of-Delft full-model result is 629.6/1171.3, exactly the ZJU result, while 1500.1/3951.8—the main View-of-Delft result—appears in the positional-embedding ablation row. In addition, the stated 38.5% View-of-Delft RMSE reduction is inconsistent with 3951.8 versus the best listed baseline value of 5385.8, which is approximately 26.6%. These errors weaken confidence in the quantitative narrative and ablations.

Reproducibility is incomplete: important architectural dimensions, prototype count, softmax axes and temperature, optimizer and batch size, input preprocessing/normalization, coefficient parameterization, validity masks, and detailed split/evaluation procedures are not fully specified. It is also unclear whether all efficiency comparisons include identical preprocessing and MDE-backbone costs.

The primary accuracy tables provide no variance across training runs or significance analysis. The Kendall-tau analysis uses a two-sample t-test on bootstrap estimates even though a paired comparison would be more appropriate. These issues do not negate the consistent multi-dataset gains, but they limit the strength of the statistical support.
